claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an fcc matrix.
The as-built alloy contains inherent elemental microsegregation or local compositional inhomogeneity.
Local compositional inhomogeneity drives differential oxide formation at the oxide–metal interface.
Differential oxide formation produces interfacial stress accumulation and decohesion.
Interfacial decohesion can trigger catastrophic cracking during high-temperature gas exposure.
Oxidation causes localized depletion of key elements, including Mn and Cr, at the oxide–metal interface.
The interface develops layered mixed oxides that may include spinel or ternary phases.
The layered mixed oxides induce significant interfacial stresses.
Accelerated high-temperature diffusion promotes growth of a heterogeneous oxide scale.
The heterogeneous oxide scale follows local chemical gradients inherited from additive-manufacturing microsegregation.
Differences in oxide growth kinetics and composition create stress concentrations at the oxide–metal interface.
Exceeding a critical interfacial stress threshold causes rapid interfacial cracking and catastrophic failure.
Increasing oxygen partial pressure causes faster and more heterogeneous oxide growth than the baseline condition.
The increased oxide growth under higher oxygen partial pressure causes greater interfacial stress and earlier crack initiation.
A reducing atmosphere slows oxidation kinetics and delays cracking relative to the baseline.
Under standard-atmosphere high-temperature exposure, the as-built alloy exhibits relatively uniform oxide growth and delayed or minimal interfacial cracking.
The proposed degradation mechanism operates over 700–900 °C when oxygen or hydrogen partial pressure is varied.

contradictions.description: The stated alloy composition contains no Mn, yet Mn depletion and the relative role of Mn versus Cr are proposed as central features of the target alloy's mechanism.

The hypothesis broadly attributes differential oxidation under high-temperature oxidizing exposure to inherent microsegregation, while the same as-built material under the standard-atmosphere baseline is said to oxidize relatively uniformly. The exposure distinction needed to reconcile these statements is not specified.
